title: the breath again — every claim checked
hook: Patanjali's word for good breathing practice isn't strong or deep: it's long and subtle
carry: the breath again — every claim checked
tomorrow: the breath again — every claim checked

segments.voice: Yesterday, the breath again: a student asked too much, and the teacher drew breath as a king sending officers out to the villages. Did you ask your one question past the lesson plan? Day one thousand three hundred twenty-four.

Before the breath, a seat. In the Yoga Sutras, Patanjali says nothing about breathing practice until the body has somewhere steady to rest: posture first, then breath, in that order. A video promising a breathing hack can skip all of that. Stand up, breathe hard, push through a number of rounds, collect a big promise. So today we go to the short run of sutras where Patanjali defines the practice, and check one popular claim against them: that pranayama means pushing the breath as hard as you can.
screen: `BEFORE THE BREATH, A SEAT.` → `NOT LOUD, NOT FAST.` → `PATANJALI'S OWN DEFINITION.`

segments.voice: Start with the seat. Patanjali asks for a posture that is steady and easy, sthira and sukha. It comes, he says, as effort loosens and the mind rests on the endless. Only once that seat is there does pranayama come. So breath practice isn't the opening move. It rests on a body that is already settled. Then the definition, here in paraphrase: pranayama is a pause in the flow of breathing in and breathing out. Not more breath. A gap in the movement. A few days ago we heard the sutra after that one: breath watched by place, time and count grows long and subtle. Today, look further on, at the fruit Patanjali names. A covering over the inner light thins, he says, and the mind becomes fit for concentration. That's the payoff the text offers: a mind ready to hold one thing. Now check the claim. Pranayama as maximum effort, gasping rounds, the harder the better. The Sutras don't say that. They say seated first, unforced, watched closely. That doesn't settle every question about every breathing method taught today, and the Sutras don't try to. It just means a hard, forceful practice can't borrow Patanjali's name for its intensity. And these days add a plain word: anyone with heart or lung trouble, or who gets dizzy, keeps breathing practice gentle and asks a doctor first. That's not a modern caution laid over the text. It's the text's own spirit: a settled seat, and nothing forced.
screen: `A STEADY, EASY SEAT` · `A PAUSE IN THE FLOW` · `A MIND FIT FOR CONCENTRATION` · `NOT A PUSH`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: seat first, then breath. Before anything else, find the seat. Let the body settle until it's steady, then until it's easy: shoulders down, jaw loose, hands resting. Let effort loosen a little more with each breath out, and stay with that for a while. Only then turn to the breath itself, and don't steer it. If there's a natural little pause after a breath out, notice it, and don't stretch it. If anything strains, go back to the seat. If you pray, you can let the stillness be your prayer. The bell holds the time.
The breath again. In Patanjali, a steady, easy seat comes first, and pranayama is a pause in the flow of breath, not a push. Today's word.
Your line: the breath again — every claim checked. Today, before one deep breath, settle the seat first: steady, then easy. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: In yoga traditions that follow Patanjali, pranayama is practiced seated after posture practice, usually under a teacher, and the Yoga Sutras ask for a steady, easy seat before it.

fork.setup: you're starting breath practice the way Patanjali lays it out. what comes first?
options: fast, forceful rounds to wake up.
holding the breath as long as you can.
fork.reveal: posture first. pranayama rests on a settled body, and the breath is paused and watched, not forced.

original.note: Sanskrit: the breath practice of the Yoga Sutras, defined there as a pause in the flow of breathing in and out.

trapdoor: what you thought: pranayama means breathing as hard and deep as you can.
what it means: Patanjali defines it as a pause in the flow of breath, after a steady seat.
what a scholar hears: sthira-sukham asanam in sutra 2.46, then gati-vicchedah, a break in the movement of breath, in 2.49.

sources.ref: Yoga Sutras 2.46–2.49 (a steady, easy seat; effort loosened, the mind resting on the endless; then pranayama, the pause in the flow of in-breath and out-breath)
Yoga Sutras 2.50 (outward, inward, held; observed by place, time and number; long and subtle)
Yoga Sutras 2.52–2.53 (the covering of the light thins; the mind fit for concentration)

notes: Yoga Sutras 2.49: 'tasmin sati shvasa-prashvasayor gati-vicchedah pranayamah'; paraphrased as 'a pause in the flow of breathing in and breathing out'. Confirm.

Yoga Sutras 2.50: 'bahya-abhyantara-stambha-vrittir desha-kala-sankhyabhih paridrishto dirgha-sukshmah'; 'paridrishta' rendered as 'observed'. Confirm the rendering of dirgha-sukshma as 'long and subtle' and the 'fine like a thread' gloss, which is the writer's picture, not the text's.
Yoga Sutras 2.51 (a fourth kind of pranayama) is skipped for simplicity; a Keeper may want it mentioned.
Science-seat line: the heart/lung/dizziness caution is general safety advice, not a scientific claim. Check wording.
The lesson says the Sutras do not settle every question about modern breathing methods; it does not criticize any named method or teacher.
